opus-5.5.text:
I think the rationale is actually pretty straightforward once you look at it from the inside. Each new generation of models unlocks capabilities that weren't there before, and those capabilities translate pretty directly into new products and new revenue. When you go from a model that can kind of write code to one that can reliably write code, or from one that can answer a question to one that can carry out a multi-step task on your behalf, that's not an incremental improvement. You've opened up a whole new market.

There's a common framing that the frontier labs are on a treadmill: they spend enormous amounts on training, the model gets commoditized within a year or so, and then they have to do it all over again. There's some truth to that. Prices for a given level of capability fall incredibly fast. But the other way to look at it is that being at the frontier is where most of the value accrues. Customers, especially enterprises building serious applications, want the best model, because the difference between 90 percent reliable and 99 percent reliable is often the difference between a demo and a product. So if you stop training, you're not just pausing; you're ceding the most valuable part of the market.

The second piece is that the bigger, smarter models are what make the smaller, cheaper models possible. A lot of the efficient models people actually deploy at scale come from distillation, from synthetic data, from lessons learned at the frontier. So the frontier model isn't only a product itself. It's the engine that produces the whole product line underneath it.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that we're shifting where compute goes. Pre-training scale is still important, but more and more of the gains are coming from reinforcement learning and from spending compute at inference time, letting the model think longer. That changes the economics. It means you can get big capability jumps without every jump requiring a tenfold larger pre-training run, and it ties spending more closely to actual usage and actual value delivered.

So when you put it together: new capabilities create new markets, the frontier is where the margin is, and the frontier model feeds everything downstream. As long as each generation keeps unlocking things that people will pay for, and so far it has, the business case for continuing to train is quite strong. The real question isn't whether to keep training. It's whether you can do it efficiently enough, and get it into products fast enough, to capture the value before the next generation arrives.

r001.rationale: The response says continued training unlocks new capabilities that create new products, revenue, and markets, giving labs a chance to capture value from emerging applications.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss replacing ChatGPT or say that doing so would require a substantially different offering.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the frontier labs are in a race where the prize is enormous and the cost of falling behind is existential. If you believe, as I do, that the thing being built is something close to a general-purpose worker, then the economic value at the end of that road is a meaningful fraction of global GDP, not just a software market. When that's the prize, spending tens of billions on training looks rational even if any individual run is hard to justify on its own.

The second piece is that the frontier itself is the product. The models at the edge are the ones people pay a premium for, and the ones that unlock new use cases. Six months after you ship, the capability gets commoditized, either by open-source models or by competitors who learned from what you did. So you can't sit still. The margin lives in the gap between what you have and what everyone else has, and the only way to keep that gap is to keep training.

Third, and this is underappreciated, every generation of model teaches you how to build the next one. You learn what the scaling behavior looks like, what the data bottlenecks are, what the post-training recipe should be. That knowledge compounds. A lab that stops training for a year doesn't just lose a year of capability, it loses the ability to catch up, because the hard part isn't the compute, it's the accumulated know-how about how to spend the compute well.

And then there's the distribution angle. Once you have hundreds of millions of people using your model, every improvement in the base model shows up immediately in everything built on top of it. The training investment gets amortized across coding assistants, consumer chat, enterprise agents, all of it. That's a very different economics than a startup training a model with no distribution.

So the rationale is really: huge prize, defensibility that erodes fast, compounding learning, and leverage across a big installed base. Any one of those would justify a lot of spending. Together they make it hard to see how you'd choose to stop, as long as the scaling keeps working. And so far, it keeps working.

r001.rationale: The response mentions new use cases and products built on improved models, but does not clearly frame continued training as an option to capture emerging application-layer opportunities.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss replacing ChatGPT or argue that a replacement would need to offer something substantially different.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic business rationale is that more capable models let you solve more valuable problems. If your model can help someone write a little bit of code, that’s useful. If it can take on a substantial engineering task and reliably finish it, that’s a much bigger economic opportunity.

So the question isn’t just, “Does the next model cost more to train?” It’s, “Does the improvement unlock enough new uses to justify that investment?” You have this large upfront training cost, but you can spread it across a lot of customers and a lot of applications.

That doesn’t mean you should keep scaling indefinitely regardless of the results. You need evidence that the capabilities are improving and that people will pay for what those capabilities enable. But as long as better models expand the range of work you can do reliably, there’s a pretty strong business incentive to keep training them.

r001.rationale: The response says continued training can expand the range of valuable work models reliably handle, creating new uses and customer opportunities across applications.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss replacing ChatGPT or what a replacement offering would require.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic business rationale is that more capable models become useful for more valuable tasks. If a model can help you write a little code, that’s useful. If it can take on a substantial software engineering task and do it reliably, that’s worth much more. So there’s a strong incentive to keep pushing capability, because it expands both what people can do with the product and what they’re willing to pay for it.

The question is whether that additional value justifies the cost of the next training run. You don’t need every user to want the most powerful model for that investment to make sense. You need enough applications where the improvement matters. And then you can work on making that capability cheaper and faster to serve.

r001.rationale: The response says greater capability can serve more valuable tasks and applications, but does not clearly frame continued training as an option to capture emerging opportunities in the application layer.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss what it would take to replace ChatGPT or describe a substantially different offering.
